passage: When Liam's email arrived, Tariq was eating toast over the sink in their Manchester flat: My first solo exhibition! Opening Friday. Tariq read it twice. Something sour rose in his chest, and a sentence formed on its own: It's only a café wall, really. He put the phone down. Okay, he thought. That's envy. He and Liam had started painting at the same evening class. Tariq had stopped after six months, busy with overtime. He picked the phone up again and wrote: Mate, that's brilliant. I'll be there Friday. Proud of you. Then, after a moment: Can I buy you a coffee after and hear how you found the time? He sent it, and pulled out the box under his bed where his paints still were.

Dear Akash,
I owe you a proper note, not just the thumbs-up I sent in the group.
When you told us your short story was accepted by the literary magazine, my first feeling wasn't joy. It was a pinch. We started writing together in college, and I've had eleven rejections this year. For a day I caught myself thinking your ending was rushed. It wasn't. It's beautiful.
So: congratulations. Really. I'm proud to know you.
And the pinch told me something useful. I've been writing less and complaining more. I want what you have, so I'm going to write every morning this month.
Would you read my next draft, when it's ready?
Aparna

passage: You want the honest version, Vaibhav? Okay. Last March, my junior from B.Ed college, Rukhsar, won the state award for young teachers. Two years younger than me. When I saw the photo, my first thought was: she only won because her school is in the city. I actually typed half of that to a friend. Then I stopped and said it out loud in my empty kitchen: Yamini, you're jealous. Just call it what it is. It felt silly, but it helped. So I deleted the message and called Rukhsar instead. I said congratulations and I meant most of it. Then I asked what she'd done in her classroom that got noticed. She laughed, said "Thank you, Didi," and told me about her reading corner for first-generation learners. And I realised the award didn't sting because of her. It stung because I've wanted to start something like that for three years and haven't.

qa.a: She won the state award for young teachers.

qa.q: What did Yamini realise the sting was really about?
qa.a: She realised it stung because she had wanted to start something similar for three years and hadn't.

qa.q: Which choice turned Yamini's envy into something useful?
qa.a: Naming the jealousy aloud, deleting the message and calling Rukhsar to ask what she did let Yamini learn from her instead of undermining her.

qa.q: What would have changed if Yamini had sent the half-typed message?
qa.a: The friend might have repeated the dig, Rukhsar could have been hurt, and Yamini would have missed what the award showed about her own goals.

passage: I'm Chinmay, and I work the grill next to Thomas at a restaurant kitchen in Kochi. Last month Chef announced that Ruth would be the new sous-chef. Ruth joined after Thomas. Jahnavi, come here. You look upset since your friend got the scholarship. Let your Vandana Aunty tell you something.
When I was twenty-five, my colleague Rekha was chosen to lead the new branch. I had wanted it badly. When I heard, my face went hot. I wanted to tell everyone she only got it because the manager liked her.

Rain was hammering the conference centre roof in Edinburgh, and Tanvir's flight home was in two hours. As he packed his laptop, the organisers announced the best paper award: Thomas, his old lab partner.
Tanvir felt his chest tighten. Their papers had been on similar topics. His thought was sharp: Thomas always gets lucky.
He stopped, bag half-zipped. That's envy, he told himself. Just envy. He had forty minutes before the taxi. He could leave quietly, or he could go and say something.
He crossed the wet courtyard to where Thomas stood with his certificate. "Well done. Honestly, I'm a bit jealous, but it's a great paper."
Thomas grinned. "Thanks, mate."
"What made the difference, do you think?"
"Real data from the field."
In the taxi, Tanvir wrote in his notes: next project, get field data.

qa.a: Thomas won the best paper award.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he heard Thomas had won?
qa.a: Tanvir felt envious, with a tight chest, and was tempted to put it down to luck.

qa.q: Which choice did Tanvir make, and why did it work?
qa.a: He named his envy, went to congratulate Thomas, and asked what made the difference, which turned the sting into a clear goal for his next project.

qa.a: Thomas seems pleased and relaxed, taking the honesty as a warm compliment.

At the book launch in a Kolkata cafe, Lavanya watched Uday sign copies of his first short-story collection and felt a sharp twist in her stomach. They had joined the same writing group four years ago. She had three unfinished stories in a folder at home. For a moment she caught herself thinking the cover was a bit plain.
She stopped. That's envy, she told herself, almost aloud.
She waited her turn, hugged him and said, "Uday, this is wonderful. I'm proud of you, and honestly a little jealous." He laughed.
"How did you finish?" she asked.
"Every morning, 6 a.m., one page."
On the metro home, Lavanya opened the oldest story on her phone and wrote one paragraph.

When my cousin Nandini told the family she had been made head nurse of her ward at twenty-six, I clapped with everyone else, and something in me went sour. I'm Payal, and I'm a nurse too, two years older. That night I noticed I'd been mentally listing her faults: bossy, lucky with her hospital.
I made myself say it plainly: I'm envious. Then I called her. "Nandini, congratulations. I mean it. And I'll be honest, I felt jealous, and I'm working through it." She was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me." I asked how she'd prepared. She had taken the ward-management course last year.
Afterwards I looked at my own goals. I don't actually want to manage a ward. I want to teach student nurses. I emailed the nursing school on Monday.

Friday night

Mahima's story got into the magazine. The real one, the one we both sent to last year. She called me first, screaming, and I screamed too. Then I put the phone down and felt sick. I've been writing longer. I was the one who told her about the magazine. For an hour I lay on the bed thinking small, ugly things: it's because of her cousin's contacts, her story isn't even that original. Then I made myself write it down properly: I am envious of Mahima. Just that. Seeing it on paper made it smaller. So I texted her: 'I'm so proud of you. Also a little jealous, honestly! Drinks on me Saturday.' She sent back ten hearts. And now I'm thinking about what it tells me: I want this too, badly. So Sunday I'm finishing the story I abandoned in March.

Jasleen
